stories.title: Cadillac F1's team boss is sacked as the team's billionaire owner faces an FBI probe — even after a record $12.5bn Lakers sale
key_points: Cadillac F1 has replaced team principal **Graeme Lowden** with **Marcin Budkowski**, described as a sacking.
Team owner **Mark Walter** is under **FBI and SEC investigation** over roughly **$16–20 billion** in undisclosed private-credit loans.
Walter's phone and computer were **seized by the FBI**; his firms received grand jury subpoenas in February.
Days earlier, Walter sold the **LA Lakers for a record $12.5 billion** — a **25% profit** in just 10 months of ownership.
The investigation does **not directly implicate** Cadillac F1 or the Dodgers, but raises questions about ownership stability.
stories.background: Mark Walter runs TWG Global and Guggenheim Partners, and his sprawling sports empire includes the LA Dodgers, the LA Lakers (until this sale), and — new to the 2026 grid — the Cadillac Formula 1 team, one of F1's newest entrants. As a brand-new team still building competitiveness, Cadillac depends heavily on stable leadership and investor confidence. The federal investigation, run by Manhattan prosecutors and the SEC, centers on roughly $16–20 billion in private-credit loans that flowed from Walter-linked insurers through third parties to entities tied to Walter or TWG Global without being properly disclosed as related-party transactions.
stories.what_happened: Cadillac unexpectedly removed team principal Graeme Lowden and replaced him with Marcin Budkowski, in a move reported as a sacking rather than a mutual decision. This coincided with mounting reports that Walter is under FBI and SEC investigation, with his phone and computer seized and his firms — including Guggenheim Partners and two insurance subsidiaries — having received grand jury subpoenas back in February. Just days before the leadership change became public, Walter agreed to sell the Lakers to Josh Kushner and former Disney chief Bob Iger for a record $12.5 billion, up from the $10 billion he paid for the team roughly 10 months earlier; the deal still needs NBA Board of Governors approval, expected in September. Reports note the federal probe does not directly touch Cadillac F1 or the Dodgers, and the teams continue operating as normal.
stories.why_it_matters: A brand-new F1 team still fighting for competitiveness now faces a leadership shake-up right as its ultimate owner is under federal scrutiny — an unusual convergence that raises real questions about long-term stability for one of the grid's 11 teams.
stories.ripple_effects: It could complicate Cadillac's pitch to sponsors, staff, and drivers about long-term stability, and puts pressure on F1's governing bodies over how they vet team owners facing legal scrutiny. Andretti's IndyCar team, also linked to TWG Global, faces similar uncertainty according to reporting.
stories.why_now: The leadership change, the federal investigation reports, and the blockbuster Lakers sale all became public within days of each other this week — an unusual convergence of sports-business news around one person.
stories.watch_next: Whether the SEC/FBI probe produces formal charges, and whether F1's governing bodies comment on Cadillac's ownership stability.

key_terms.definition: A financial deal between entities that are connected (e.g., owned by the same person), which regulators require to be clearly disclosed to avoid hidden conflicts of interest.

stories.the_lesson: Sports team ownership is increasingly tied to sprawling, leveraged corporate empires — a federal investigation into an owner's unrelated business dealings can create real uncertainty for a team's fans and staff, even when the team itself isn't accused of wrongdoing.
stories.market_link: Any formal charges against Walter's Guggenheim-linked entities could ripple into insurance and private-credit markets well beyond sports.

stories.title: Formula 1's teenage title leader goes undercover at a German karting event — and wins
key_points: Mercedes' **Kimi Antonelli**, F1's **19-year-old championship leader**, raced go-karts in Germany under the alias 'Franz Antonelli.'
The fake name is a **direct nod to Max Verstappen**, who used 'Franz Hermann' to race incognito in 2025.
Antonelli reportedly **smashed rival competitors' lap times** despite the disguise.
He heads into next week's **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** holding a **50-point championship lead** over Lewis Hamilton.
The stunt keeps alive an unofficial F1 tradition of stars **racing incognito** between race weekends.
stories.background: Kimi Antonelli was promoted to Mercedes' race seat and has become the sport's breakout story in 2026, becoming the youngest points leader in F1 history at just 19. The 'racing incognito' tradition traces back to Max Verstappen, who first used the pseudonym 'Franz Hermann' in May 2025 to enter karting events without drawing a crowd. Formula 1 is on its summer break before resuming at Zandvoort for the Dutch Grand Prix — confirmed as the venue's final scheduled appearance on the calendar after five years back on the F1 schedule, and the first time the race will run as a Sprint weekend.
stories.what_happened: Antonelli entered a karting event in Germany under the alias 'Franz Antonelli' — a play on Verstappen's own pseudonym — reportedly outpacing other competitors at the session despite trying to stay under the radar. The appearance came in the closing days of F1's summer break, just before the grid reconvenes for the Dutch Grand Prix weekend at Zandvoort on August 21–23, where Antonelli will defend a 50-point lead over second-placed Lewis Hamilton and a 59-point lead over his own teammate George Russell.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a light story, but it underscores just how dominant and competitively restless Antonelli's title-winning form has been in 2026 — even on a break, the championship leader can't stay off a track.
stories.ripple_effects: It adds fan and media buzz ahead of Zandvoort's historic farewell Sprint weekend, and offers a lighter counter-narrative to the driver-market chaos that has otherwise dominated F1 headlines this summer.
stories.why_now: It happened in the final days before F1's summer break ends and the Zandvoort weekend begins.
stories.watch_next: Whether Antonelli extends his championship lead at Zandvoort's Sprint weekend, August 21–23.
stories.the_lesson: Even in F1's most data-driven, simulator-trained era, drivers still go racing for fun on their days off — competitive instinct doesn't clock out just because the championship points are already banked.

stories.title: Red Bull fends off Cadillac's approach for chief engineer Paul Monaghan with a counteroffer
key_points: Red Bull has reportedly kept veteran chief engineer **Paul Monaghan** from leaving for **Cadillac** by matching or beating its offer.
Monaghan, nicknamed **'Pedals'** in the paddock, has spent years in senior Red Bull technical roles and was back in the garage at the **Hungarian Grand Prix**.
Cadillac, F1's newest team, has been aggressively **poaching experienced engineering talent** from established outfits as it builds its operation from scratch.
The episode is part of a wider pattern this season of new and expanding teams raiding rivals' technical staff, not just their drivers.
stories.background: When a new Formula 1 team joins the grid — as Cadillac did this season — it typically has no existing engineering department, so it has to build one almost entirely by hiring away experienced staff from established rivals, often at a significant pay premium. This kind of quiet personnel story rarely gets headlines the way driver transfers do, but senior race and design engineers can matter just as much to a car's competitiveness. Paul Monaghan has spent years in senior technical roles at Red Bull, one of the grid's most successful teams, giving him exactly the pedigree a new team like Cadillac would want.
stories.what_happened: Reports suggested Paul Monaghan was on the verge of leaving Red Bull for **Cadillac**, F1's newest team, as it builds out its technical department ahead of a fuller 2027 push. Red Bull responded with a **counteroffer** substantial enough to persuade the **58-year-old** to stay, according to paddock reporting, and he was back working in the Red Bull garage at the **Hungarian Grand Prix** in Budapest. The near-miss underscores how aggressively Cadillac has been recruiting experienced engineering and technical staff from rival teams as it tries to compress years of institutional knowledge into a much shorter build-up.
stories.why_it_matters: Engineering talent is as competitive a market in F1 as drivers, and losing a senior figure like Monaghan would have been a real blow to Red Bull's technical continuity heading into the 2027 rules reset — while a win for Cadillac would have accelerated its credibility as a serious operation, not just a name on the grid.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect more of this kind of tug-of-war as Cadillac and other newer or expanding outfits continue poaching technical staff from established teams through the rest of the season, and established teams like Red Bull to respond with retention pay rises to protect their institutional knowledge.
stories.why_now: This is surfacing now because teams are locking in personnel for the 2027 regulation change over the summer break, the same window driving the wider driver-market frenzy.
stories.watch_next: Whether Cadillac lands other senior engineering hires from rival teams before the 2027 rules take effect.
stories.the_lesson: Competitiveness in a technical sport isn't just about who's driving the car — the engineers and staff who never appear on a podium are often worth as much of a fight as the star names.

stories.title: F1's 2027 driver market blows wide open: only 8 of 22 seats are filled
key_points: F1 has officially confirmed only **8 of the 22 seats** on the 2027 grid are locked in, with **14 seats** still undecided.
**Max Verstappen's** exit clause in his Red Bull contract is now active, and he's been publicly **warned about the downsides** of a rumoured move to McLaren.
**Audi** has moved to shore up its lineup, with Gabriel Bortoleto's camp shutting down exit talk and Nico Hülkenberg expected to partner him.
The uncertainty spans midfield and top teams alike, with **Carlos Sainz's** Williams future among several other seats still unresolved.
2026's 'silly season' is unusually wide open because so many contracts were written to expire together at the end of this year.
stories.background: Formula 1 driver contracts typically run one to three years, and a cluster of them were signed to expire at the end of **2026** — meaning an unusually large share of the 22-driver grid is up for renegotiation at once heading into 2027. Complicating things further, F1's new technical regulations take effect in 2027, prompting teams to rethink which drivers best suit the new cars before locking in long-term deals. Max Verstappen, a four-time champion, has an **exit clause** in his Red Bull contract tied to team performance that has now become active, making him the single biggest variable in the market and drawing interest from rivals including McLaren.
stories.what_happened: An official F1 update confirmed that just **8 of the 22 seats** on the 2027 grid are currently filled, leaving **14 seats** open with the season not even past its summer-break halfway point. The update reaffirmed Max Verstappen's status: his Red Bull exit clause is active, and he's reportedly been warned by people close to the sport about the downsides of a move to McLaren, where seat politics and an already title-winning lineup could complicate his fit. Elsewhere, Audi's driver picture firmed up slightly — Gabriel Bortoleto's camp shut down speculation about an exit, saying his contract has **'no clauses,'** while veteran Nico Hülkenberg is expected to continue alongside him. Meanwhile Carlos Sainz's future at Williams and several other seats, including at teams still finalising 2027 plans, remain unresolved.
stories.why_it_matters: A driver market this open, this early, is unusual for F1 — it means the sport's biggest names, led by Verstappen, could realistically switch teams for 2027, reshaping the competitive order just as new technical rules land. For fans and sponsors, uncertainty at the top creates ripple effects all the way down the grid, since every seat Verstappen might vacate or fill triggers a chain of other moves.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect a summer and autumn of intense driver-market speculation, with teams racing to lock in talent before rivals do. Sponsors and manufacturers, including Audi and Cadillac as they build out new programs, have extra incentive to finalize lineups quickly to plan marketing around them, while smaller teams risk losing leverage if star drivers wait out their options.
stories.why_now: The story is trending now because F1 is at its summer break — the traditional lull when contract talks, rumours and 'transfer roundups' dominate the news cycle before racing resumes at the Dutch Grand Prix.
stories.watch_next: Whether Verstappen commits to Red Bull through 2028, as some reports suggest he's expected to confirm at the Dutch Grand Prix, or activates his exit clause instead.

key_terms.definition: A condition written into a driver's contract that lets them leave early — often triggered by the team failing to hit a performance target, like finishing outside a certain championship position.

stories.the_lesson: In any market where contracts cluster around the same expiry date, uncertainty compounds — one big name's decision can freeze or unlock dozens of smaller moves down the chain.
